H1: Task A and Task B minimum rate change scores will be positively correlated.

table.study_design_overview:
Within-Subjects Design. All participants will complete 2 Breathing Tasks measuring Interoceptive Awareness (Task A & Task B), subjective confidence and arousal questions following each trial, and a MAIA questionnaire.  Order of performing Task A and Task B will be counterbalanced across participants. 

Task A:  In this task participants will be asked to match their breath to a circle on a computer screen that expands and contracts rhythmically. Pulse rate will always start at 5-seconds/pulse. Participants will also be asked to indicate through a key press the beginning of every inhale and exhale. This offers a behavioral measure that indicates their ability to match their breathing rate with the pulsing circle. Each trial will consist of 8- circle pulses. As discovered in a previous pilot study (Farb & Logie, 2018) if the pulse of the circle is changed gradually with each breath, on average participants awareness of respiration change is no greater than chance levels even when the overall change is as large as 65% from initial breathing rate. Awareness of change is determined through a 3-way forced choice question after each trial (“On the previous trial did your breathing rate increase, decrease, or stay constant?”). For the current study, we are interested in calculating a threshold of awareness of change in respiration. To do so, a staircase method will be used, such that the overall change in respiration rate over the full trial will either increase or decrease (using a 1-up, 2-down rule) based upon correct or incorrect response on the previous trial. 2 correct responses in a row will lead to a step down in the staircase while 1 incorrect response will lead to one step easier. Step sizes represent total increase or decrease in respiration rate from the previous position on the staircase. The first level of overall respiration rate change will be 50% over the 8 pulses. Speed-up, Slow-down as well as “no-change” trials will be used [1/3 of total trials for each] so that the pulse rate is not changing every time. 

Task B. In this task participants will also match their breath to a circle on a computer screen that expands and contracts rhythmically. Pulse rate will always start at 5-seconds/pulse. Participants will also be asked to indicate through a key press when they begin each inhale and exhale. However in this task participants will be asked to press the spacebar once they notice that their breathing rate has changed.  “No change” trials, in which the rate of the pulses stays constant the entire duration of the trial, will be randomly interspersed so that the pulse rate is not changing every time. In total there will be 4 “no-change”, 4 speed-up and 4 slow-down trials randomly presented. The maximum number of pulses for each trial will be capped at 12.

table.title: The Interoceptive Change Awareness Task (ICAT): A New Paradigm for Investigating Interoception
table.research_questions:
Inferential Hypotheses

H1. The threshold for correctly detecting change on acceleration trials will be lower (easier) than detection of deceleration trials 

H2. The threshold for correctly detecting change on high salience trials will be lower (easier) than detection of low salience trials 

H3. Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT) and adaptive interoception (MAIA scores)
H3A: BCAT confidence scores will be positively related to MAIA scores
H3B: BCAT threshold scores not be related to MAIA scores

H4. Subjective arousal will positively correlated with the magnitude of respiratory change; specifically:
H4A: there will be a positive relationship between magnitude of respiratory change and arousal, such that greater frequency of breathing is linked to greater arousal
H4B: The relationship between subjective arousal and respiratory change will be moderated by detection accuracy, such that the relationship will be stronger when respiratory change is accurately detected
H4C: The relationship between subjective arousal and respiratory change will be moderated by task instruction, such that it will be stronger in following breath instructions than following visual instructions

H5. When using the thresholds estimated in the learning trials, an independent block of test trials that vary salience while holding the change level at the participant’s high salience threshold will be effective in manipulating detection accuracy. 

Descriptive Hypotheses

H6. Test retest reliability will be at least good (r = .7 or higher), and lower within the visual instruction first condition than the consistent breath instruction condition

table.study_design_overview:
Study Design:
The purpose of the study is to validate a novel task for measuring individual differences in breath awareness, specifically the ability to detect changes in breathing rate and the confidence associated with detection judgments. The study is mostly a within-participant design, featuring the Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT), a heartbeat counting task, and self-questionnaires assessing interoceptive awareness, self-confidence, and subjective well-being. 

Participants will attend a single 1 hour laboratory session, in which they will complete informed consent and be outfitted with respiration and heartbeat monitors. They will then perform the BCAT, the heartbeat counting task, self-report questionnaires, and then the BCAT again to assess test-retest reliability.

The BCAT features a learning phase that has two main factors: (1) direction/magnitude of respiratory change [faster/slower/no change], and (2) the salience of the change [high/low]. Following each BCAT paced breathing trial (see materials for details), participants will engage in a three-alternative forced choice around change detection. The magnitude of change will be determined by a psychophysics staircase to estimate participant’s ability to detect change in respiration rate. The BCAT then features a testing phase in which participants will be assessed at their high salience threshold while manipulating trial salience to verify whether the participant thresholds have been correctly estimated. 

Between-Participant Randomization: to determine the extent to which task performance can be explained by visual detection alone, participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions: visual and breath. In the [breath] condition participants will receive normal BCAT instructions before each of the BCAT tasks; in the [visual] condition, participants will first be instructed only to view the circle’s changing rate, with no reference to the breath; then, upon the repetition of the BCAT, all participants will be told to breath along with the circle and join their breath.

Within-Participant Randomization: the BCAT features within participant randomization as the order of the 4 different staircase conditions (deceleration low salience, deceleration high salience, acceleration low salience, acceleration high salience) will be counterbalanced randomly by participant. Breath Change Awareness Task. A three-alternative forced choice task that employs a psychophysics staircase to estimate participant’s ability to detect change in respiration rate. 

Training Trials: Participants are presented with trials in which their breathing rate either increases or decreases over four breaths, with changes occurring either gradually or quickly. After each trial, participants are asked to identify whether their breathing rate increased or decreased, rate their confidence in the accuracy of their response, and report their level of wakefulness or arousal. Four distinct conditions are used: high salience (rapid changes) and low salience (gradual changes) for both acceleration and deceleration of breathing. 

For high salience trials, the change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration in a single multiplication between pulse 2 and 3: New duration = Old Duration * Change Amount

For low salience trials, the local (pulse specific) change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration between every pulse using the following calculation:
LocalChange= ChangeAmount ^ 1/(numBreaths -1) 

Test trials: Following the staircase for the four conditions, the high salience thresholds will be used for 16 test trials. The test trials will evenly split direction type: i.e., they will consist of 8 acceleration and 8 deceleration trials. Within each direction, there will be 4 high salience and 4 low salience trials. However, the threshold will be set consistently at the high salience threshold for that direction across all 8 trials. We would therefore expect accuracy to decrease for low salience trials as generally the high salience threshold will be too difficult to detect in a low salience trial presentation.

Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether the breathing rate has increased or decreased after each trial by comparing their response to the actual change that occurred. 

Confidence: the self-reported certainty a participant has in their assessment of whether the breathing rate increased or decreased after each trial.

Arousal: self-reported level of alertness after each trial to capture the subjective experience of perceived difficulty or the extent to which the change in breathing rate captured their attention.

Stress. The Brief Inventory of Perceived Stress (BIPS; Lehman et al., 2012) is a 9 item questionnaire that assesses stress across three dimensions: lack of control, conflict and imposition, and pushed (3 questions per subscale). The questionnaire items are rated on a 5-point scale (0 = Never, 4 = Very Often) similar to the two stress questionnaires - Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) and Perceived Stress Questionnaire (PSQ) - BIPS is derived from. At the 1-month and 1-year mark, the BIPS test-retest reliabilities were comparable to those of the PSS.

Graphic emoji ratings: Created by Norman Farb, PhD to assess 4 measures - alertness (tired - wired), sad - happy, relaxed - stressed, and life satisfaction - on a 6-point scale. The emoticons are unvalidated but used as experimental quick assessment measures.

The Perth Alexithymia Questionnaire-Short Form (PAQ-S; Preece et al., 2023) is a brief, 6-item measure designed to assess alexithymia, a trait involving difficulties with recognizing and articulating emotions, and a tendency to focus on external events over internal experiences. table.indices:
Group: the between group assignment to do the first BCAT normally (Breath condition), or as a visual control condition, to be instructed only to view the circle’s changing rate, with no reference to the breath; then, upon the repetition of the BCAT, participants will be told to breath along with the circle and join their breath (Visual condition).

Detection Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether their breathing accelerated or decelerated after each trial compared to the actual change that occurred. 

Direction: whether a given trial involves acceleration or deceleration of the respiratory rate. A -1 indicates acceleration, and a 1 indicates deceleration

Level: the proportion change in the circle pulse duration from the start to the end of the trial. For example a 30% acceleration or deceleration is a level of .3

Magnitude of Respiratory Change: the degree of variation in the breathing rate, specifically the extent of acceleration and deceleration, observed across trials. This measures how large or significant the change in breathing rate is as determined by the psychophysical staircase method, which adjusts based on the participant’s correct or incorrect assessment of whether their breathing rate has increased or decreased. It is formally calculated as Direction * Level, so an acceleration of 30% = -1 * .3 = -.3, where as a deceleration of 30% = 1 * .3 = .3; this allows for the total change amount to be calculated as 1 + the magnitude of change.

Salience: how easily noticeable the change in breathing rate is after each trial. Either a gradual change in breathing rate (low salience) or marked change in breathing rate (high salience). 

Threshold: the minimum change in respiratory acceleration or deceleration required for a participant to reliably detect a shift in breathing rate. This threshold is determined using a psychophysical staircase procedure, where stimulus intensity is adaptively adjusted based on performance. A lower threshold indicates greater sensitivity, indicating that a participant can detect smaller changes in breathing rates, whereas a higher threshold suggests reduced sensitivity, requiring larger changes for detection. This measure serves as an index of interoceptive precision in the context of respiratory perception. The threshold score is calculated as the average of the last 2 trials in the staircase for any given condition.

Arousal: a participant’s self-reported level of emotional activation in response to each breathing rate trial. Arousal is assessed using a 6-point graphic rating scale featuring emoji representations, allowing participants to gauge their internal state. This measure captures an individual’s perceived intensity of arousal in response to changes in breathing rate.

Confidence: a participant’s self-assessed certainty in their judgement of whether the breathing rate accelerated or decelerated during a given trial. Confidence is measured using a 6-point numeric scale, with higher ratings indicating greater certainty in the accuracy of their response. This measure provides insight into a participants’ meta-perceptual awareness, reflecting their ability to evaluate the reliability of their interoceptive judgements. 

Adaptive Interoception: an individual’s ability to accurately perceive and interpret internal bodily sensations in a way that supports effective self-regulation and well-being. It reflects the capacity to detect and differentiate between accelerations and decelerations in breathing rate. Sensitivity to internal physiological changes is indicative of refined interoceptive awareness, allowing individuals to appropriately respond to bodily cues and adjust their physiological or emotional states accordingly.

Most analyses (H1, H2, H4, H5) will employ multilevel linear models as implemented using the ‘lme4’ package in the R statistical programming environment. As this is a fully within-participants design, the models will nest data within participant IDs.

H1. The threshold for correctly detecting change on acceleration trials will be lower (easier) than detection of deceleration trials 

Model.H1 = lmer(Threshold ~ Direction + (1 | ParticipantID), data = dataset)
The critical term is the parameter estimate for Direction.

H2. The threshold for correctly detecting change on high salience trials will be lower (easier) than detection of low salience trials 

Model.H2 = lmer(Threshold ~ Salience + (1 | ParticipantID), data = dataset)
The critical term is the parameter estimate for Salience.

H3. Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT) and adaptive interoception (MAIA scores)
H3A: BCAT confidence scores will be positively related to MAIA scores
H3B: BCAT threshold scores not be related to MAIA scores

Model.H3A = cor.test(dataset$Confidence, dataset$MAIA)
Model.H3B = cor.test(dataset$Threshold, dataset$MAIA)

The critical term here is the correlation coefficient. Because we cannot estimate the strength of the null using frequentist statistics, we will also employ Bayesian stats to estimate the strength of the null for Threshold and MAIA, expecting a Bayes factor of 3 or more in favour of the null hypothesis (no relationship.

H4. Subjective arousal will positively correlated with the magnitude of respiratory change; specifically:
H4A: there will be a positive relationship between magnitude of respiratory change and arousal, such that greater frequency of breathing is linked to greater arousal
H4B: The relationship between subjective arousal and respiratory change will be moderated by detection accuracy, such that the relationship will be stronger when respiratory change is accurately detected
H4C: The relationship between subjective arousal and respiratory change will be moderated by task instruction, such that it will be stronger in following breath instructions than following visual instructions

Model.H4A = lmer(Arousal ~ Change + (1 | id), 
                data = dataset)

The critical term is the fixed effect of Change

Model.H4B = lmer(Arousal ~ Change*Accuracy + (1 | id),

The critical term is the fixed interaction effect of Change*Accuracy

Model.H4C = lmer(Arousal ~ Change*Group + (1 | id), 
                 data = dataset)

The critical term is the fixed interaction effect of Change*Group

H5. When using the thresholds estimated in the learning trials, an independent block of test trials that vary salience while holding the change level at the participant’s high salience threshold will be effective in manipulating detection accuracy. 

Model.H5 = lmer(Accuracy ~ Salience + (1 | id), data = longTest)
The critical term is the fixed effect of salience on the test trials

Training Trials: Participants are presented with trials in which their breathing rate either increases or decreases over four breaths, with changes occurring either gradually or quickly. After each trial, participants are asked to identify whether their breathing rate increased or decreased, rate their confidence in the accuracy of their response, and report their level of wakefulness or arousal. Four distinct conditions are used: high salience (rapid changes) and low salience (gradual changes) for both acceleration and deceleration of breathing.

For high salience trials, the change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration in a single multiplication between pulse 2 and 3: New duration = Old Duration * Change Amount

For low salience trials, the local (pulse specific) change amount is applied to the circle pulse duration between every pulse using the following calculation:
LocalChange= ChangeAmount ^ 1/(numBreaths -1)

Test trials: Following the staircase for the four conditions, the high salience thresholds will be used for 16 test trials. The test trials will evenly split direction type: i.e., they will consist of 8 acceleration and 8 deceleration trials. Within each direction, there will be 4 high salience and 4 low salience trials. However, the threshold will be set consistently at the high salience threshold for that direction across all 8 trials. We would therefore expect accuracy to decrease for low salience trials as generally the high salience threshold will be too difficult to detect in a low salience trial presentation.

Accuracy: participant’s ability to correctly assess whether the breathing rate has increased or decreased after each trial by comparing their response to the actual change that occurred.

Confidence: the self-reported certainty a participant has in their assessment of whether the breathing rate increased or decreased after each trial.

Arousal: self-reported level of alertness after each trial to capture the subjective experience of perceived difficulty or the extent to which the change in breathing rate captured their attention.

text.text: The Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA) measures adaptive interoceptive sensibility (attention to the body and how one appraises it) and predicts mental health; how that disposition shows up during a bodily task has rarely been tested.

We asked whether MAIA scores predict accuracy, confidence or their coupling in the Breath Change Awareness Task, in which participants breathe along with a visual pacer, report whether its pace changed and rate confidence on every trial.

Across five samples (N = 687; in Study 5, a respiratory belt confirmed breathing along in 145 of 170 recorded participants), MAIA scores predicted mean confidence (metacognitive bias) in every sample (pooled r = .27, 95% CI [.17, .37]), including Study 5's preregistered test (r = .26 [.13, .38]; Breath blocks only, r = .26).

They were not positively related to perceptual sensitivity (how well changes were detected) or to metacognitive sensitivity, how well confidence tracked accuracy: pooled, positive relations of r = .10 or more were ruled out for both.
Study 5's preregistered detection-threshold null, a stricter criterion, was not established (BF₀₁ = 2.2, below the required 3).
In Study 5, the association held with self-esteem, self-doubt, alexithymia and affect controlled.

It was also present with vision alone (following the pacer by eye without breathing along), which should weaken a body-based link: r = .22 [.01, .41], with no detectable difference from breathing along (.20).
During sensory discrimination, adaptive sensibility showed up as confidence, independent of accuracy and present even without breathing along.

The Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA; Mehling et al., 2012 Mehling et al., , 2018) measures interoceptive sensibility (Garfinkel et al., 2015): how often people attend to the body and how they appraise what they notice.

text.text: It is not a measure of perceptual skill: trait mindfulness is largely unrelated to objective body awareness (Treves et al., 2019), and MAIA subscales were unrelated to cardiac and respiratory task performance but related to confidence on both (Banellis et al., 2026).

text.text: The MAIA was not positively related to metacognitive sensitivity in any sample: BF₀₁ = 3.2 to 4.1 in four samples, and in Study 5 r = -.16 [-.30, -.01].
Pooled, r = -.09 [-.21, .03], and a positive relation of .10 or more was excluded (one-sided p = .006).
In the trial-level models, higher MAIA scores went with higher confidence in all five samples (b = 0.09 to 0.22 SD per SD, all p ≤ .034).
The association held with the no-change false-alarm rate partialed out (Supplement S15), so the bias does not reflect a liberal "changed" criterion.

The MAIA did not strengthen the accuracy-confidence relation: the interaction was negative in four samples and significant in none (b = -0.07 to 0.02); pooled, b = -0.04 [-0.08, 0.01], p = .10 (sample estimates), and -0.03 [-0.07, -0.002], p = .04 (one model).
Other checks agreed (Supplement S15).
The association showed no detectable weakening with vision alone.

For Visual-first participants in Study 5 (n = 90), the MAIA predicted confidence about equally with vision alone (r = .22 [.01, .41]) and when breathing along (r = .20 [-.01, .39]; Williams t(87) = -0.33, p = .74); corrected for order with the Breath-first group (n = 66), Breath -Visual = -.04 [-.22, .16].
text.formatted: For Visual-first participants in Study 5 (n = 90), the MAIA predicted confidence about equally with vision alone (r = .22 [.01, .41]) and when breathing along (r = .20 [-.01, .39]; Williams t(87) = -0.33, p = .74); corrected for order with the Breath-first group (n = 66), Breath -Visual = -.04 <ref type="bibr">[-.22, .16</ref>].

text.text: Their confidence correlated .80 across blocks, and with Visual-block confidence partialed out, the MAIA correlated .04 with Breath-block confidence (Supplement S6).
Between groups it was somewhat weaker with vision alone, but not reliably: Study 4, .35 (Breath) vs. .14 (Visual); Study 5 Block 1, .29 vs. .22; combined, Δz = 0.13 [-0.09, 0.35], p = .23.
Neither between-group comparison isolates breathing: post hoc, Study 5's groups differed more when both breathed along in Block 2 (Breath-first .40 vs.
Visual-first .20), and Study 4's breathing was not recorded.

In Study 5, the association held when controlling for self-esteem and self-doubt, the preregistered exploratory control (partial r = .22), and, unplanned, for alexithymia (.26), affect (.19) and all together (r = .19 [.04, .33]).
Distress controls, also unplanned, left partial r = .27 (Study 5), .36 (Study 2) and .33 (Study 4; Table S18).
text.formatted: Distress controls, also unplanned, left partial r = .27 (Study 5), .36 (Study 2) and .33 (Study 4; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S18</ref>).

text.text: A second body-awareness questionnaire, the BARQ-R (higher scores, poorer awareness; Dragesund et al., 2018), did not predict confidence (Study 5: r = -.04, BF₀₁ = 5.0).

text.text: Interoceptive Awareness) total with three task measures, by sample: confidence (metacognitive bias), metacognitive sensitivity (type-2 AUROC) and perceptual sensitivity (the sign-reversed threshold; in Study 3, proportion correct against the change actually displayed, reconstructed after a coding defect).
Positive values mean that higher MAIA scores went with higher confidence or better performance.
Breath condition; every participant in the sample.

The pooled row is the random-effects estimate on Fisher-z, counting each person once (diamond, Hartung-Knapp 95% CI with the ad hoc correction), with its 95% prediction interval (line; equal to the CI where I² = 0). n at the right of each row; fewer participants have an AUROC (at least five correct and five incorrect trials) or a threshold (thresholds: Study 4, 55 of 63; Study 5, 180 of 183).
Across five samples, people with higher MAIA scores were more confident in their breathing-change judgments, but no better at detecting the changes or telling correct from incorrect.
In Study 5, exploratorily, confidence went with positive affect more than with distress, and affect controls lowered the association, whereas distress controls barely moved it (Tables S18-S19).
text.formatted: In Study 5, exploratorily, confidence went with positive affect more than with distress, and affect controls lowered the association, whereas distress controls barely moved it (Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S18-S19</ref>).

text.text: With the BARQ-R reversed, both body-awareness questionnaires went with less distress and more positive affect (Studies 4-5), but only the MAIA detectably predicted confidence.
The MAIA's six general-factor subscales shared the association; none carried it alone (Supplement S9).
The total without the Trusting subscale correlated .26 with confidence (Supplement S10).

A disposition toward confidence that showed no detectable weakening with vision alone fits evidence that average confidence is stable across tasks and domains (Ais et al., 2016; Kelemen et al., 2000; Mazancieux et al., 2020).

text.text: MAIA subscales likewise went with confidence on cardiac and respiratory tasks (Banellis et al., 2026).
text.formatted: MAIA subscales likewise went with confidence on cardiac and respiratory tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Banellis et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The samples used three MAIA versions and evolving task designs, in sequence, not as independent replications.
Because detection could draw on vision, perceptual sensitivity here is change detection in this task, not necessarily respiratory accuracy.
Type-2 AUROC rests on modest trial counts, especially in Study 1.
Every pooled estimate holds without Study 3, whose displayed changes were reconstructed (Table 1; Table S4).
text.formatted: Every pooled estimate holds without Study 3, whose displayed changes were reconstructed (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>; Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Pooled, the data rule out observed positive relations of .10 or more with detection and metacognitive sensitivity, but not negative ones, nor a Breath-Visual difference of .10.
Both measures are self-report, and in Studies 1-2 agreement style predicted confidence alongside the MAIA's shared content (Supplement S7); the Brief MAIA-2 cannot separate the two.
Partialing out arousal, rated like confidence, barely changed the association, and it held in Study 4, where the MAIA came before the task.
The MAIA tracked confidence: present in every sample, intact under Study 5's controls, present with vision alone, and independent of accuracy.
Adaptive interoceptive sensibility shows up during sensory discrimination as trust in one's judgments rather than as perceptual skill.
Whether that trust carries part of sensibility's clinical benefits (Khalsa et al., 2018) is the next question.
